  "headline_index": 4,
  "what_the_study_did": "The study investigated the impact of refining gene pathways and incorporating gene expression data on the prediction performance of drug-induced side effects using the PathFX algorithm.",
  "what_it_found": "Refining pathways and incorporating gene expression data can reduce overprediction and enhance preclinical prediction of drug-induced safety events, with performance varying by side effect.",
  "key_quotes": [
    {
      "quote": "While attractive, PPI network methods have some limitations, yet they may still be useful in development pipelines. Network models tend to overpredict drug phenotypes and there is insufficient evidence to validate these predictions.",
      "topic": "PPI method limitations"
    },
    {
      "quote": "Yet, a meta-analysis of the predictive values of in vivo animal models for drug side effect prediction achieved sensitivity and specificity ranges of 0.00–0.74 and 0.33–1.00 depending on the organ categories and species.",
      "topic": "Animal model performance"
    },
    {
      "quote": "We also discovered that a per‐pathway phenotype assessment enhanced prediction accuracy and reduced overprediction.",
      "topic": "Pathway assessment"
    },
    {
      "quote": "Pathway engineering can reduce overprediction of drug‐induced side effects and increase sensitivity when side effect pathways are poorly defined",
      "topic": "Pathway engineering"
    },
    {
      "quote": "All engineered pathways had improved specificity compared with the baseline analysis.",
      "topic": "Improved specificity"
    },
    {
      "quote": "We compared our results to Monticello et al. 4 which collected preclinical and clinical rates of side effects by organ system (e.g., “cardiovascular” or “gastrointestinal”) and reported sensitivity and specificity of three animal models—“rodent,” “dogs,” and “non‐human primates”—for their ability to anticipate clinical side effects (Figure 5 ).",
      "topic": "Comparison to animal models"
    }
  ]
}
